slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 5: Understanding Move Semantics. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 5, treat 5.1.2 Identifying Temporary Values as a design decision with costs and evidence. A temporary value can initialize an owning destination directly, and many return-value situations benefit from guaranteed or permitted copy elision. Do not insert std::move into every return statement; it can interfere with useful elision in cases where returning the local by name is the right expression. An xvalue designates an object whose resources may be reused by a move-aware operation. std::move(existing) produces such a cast result; it does not itself call the object’s move constructor. The receiving operation still determines what happens. A const source often cannot supply the mutable source required by an ordinary ownership-transferring move. The custom buffer has coupled members: its size describes the allocation owned by its unique pointer.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 5, treat 5.2.1 Implementing Move Constructors as a design decision with costs and evidence. The move constructor transfers the unique pointer and uses std::exchange to replace the source size with zero. This preserves the source’s empty-buffer invariant while the destination receives the previous size and allocation. Simply defaulting the move would transfer the unique pointer but copy the scalar size, leaving the source with a positive size and no storage. That would make its checked accessor’s size test misleading. A defaulted operation is correct only when the memberwise result preserves the enclosing invariant; Rule of Zero works best when the representation itself composes cleanly. slides.title: 5.2.2 Implementing Move Assignment
keyPoints: Move assignment begins with an already-live destination, so it must release or replace the destination’s old.
Assigning the unique pointer handles that release, while exchanging the source size completes the coupled-state.
Move assignment begins with an already-live destination, so it must release or replace the destination’s old.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 5, treat 5.2.2 Implementing Move Assignment as a design decision with costs and evidence. Move assignment begins with an already-live destination, so it must release or replace the destination’s old resource as well as acquire the source’s resource. Assigning the unique pointer handles that release, while exchanging the source size completes the coupled-state transfer. The example guards self-move assignment explicitly. Both move operations are declared noexcept because their member operations are nonthrowing for this representation. This promise can affect container strategies for relocating elements; do not add noexcept to an operation that may actually propagate an exception, since an escaping exception would terminate the program. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 5, treat Trace both objects, not only the destination as a design decision with costs and evidence. Write the buffer’s representation beside each operation: size and ownership. Before the first move, the source owns three zero-initialized integers, one of which is changed to 42. After move construction, the destination owns that allocation and the source has size zero with no allocation. Reassigning the source establishes a new resource independent of the transferred one. The vector demonstration then transfers buffers into a larger owner. The vector owns buffer objects; each buffer owns its own integer allocation. These are two ownership levels. A vector reallocation can move the buffer objects without copying their underlying integer arrays because the buffer’s move operation transfers that inner ownership. slides.title: Failure clinic — A nonzero size with no storage
keyPoints: A defaulted move operation can be wrong for a representation with redundant or coupled state.
If one member owns storage and another independently records its length, moving the owner and copying the scalar.
The fix is either a custom move that repairs the relationship or a simpler representation whose size is derived.
For an application class containing only a vector, querying vector.size() avoids maintaining a second length.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 5, treat Failure clinic — A nonzero size with no storage as a design decision with costs and evidence. A defaulted move operation can be wrong for a representation with redundant or coupled state. If one member owns storage and another independently records its length, moving the owner and copying the scalar may leave the source’s invariant broken. The fix is either a custom move that repairs the relationship or a simpler representation whose size is derived from the owning member. For an application class containing only a vector, querying vector.size() avoids maintaining a second length. That representation can support the Rule of Zero. The custom buffer retains the pair deliberately to teach why moving members individually is not the same as validating the enclosing object. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

question.answer: Move assignment begins with an already-live destination, so it must release or replace the destination’s old resource as well as acquire the source’s resource. Assigning the unique pointer handles that release, while exchanging the source size completes the coupled-state transfer.
